title: Supreme Court Orders Release of Minors, Bars Coercive Action as NEET Crisis Deepens
excerpt: The bench warned against police excesses against student protesters and may constitute an SIT led by a former SC judge to probe brutality allegations.
body:
• India's Supreme Court ordered the release of all under-18 protesters detained during NEET paper leak demonstrations and barred states from taking coercive action against students.
  • The CBI has filed charges against 13 people, including three NTA subject experts and coaching institute associates, in connection with the leaked exam papers.
  • The bench indicated it may constitute a Special Investigation Team headed by a former Supreme Court judge to probe allegations of police brutality during protests.
  • The weeks-long agitation ended after Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned, but the court warned that "listening to youth is the most powerful force to prevent protest violence."

India's Supreme Court intervened forcefully in the escalating NEET paper leak crisis this week, ordering states to release minors detained during student protests and restraining law enforcement from taking coercive action against demonstrators — even as federal investigators filed formal charges against 13 people linked to the leaked exam.

Court Orders Release of Detained Minors

A bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, joined by Justices Joymala Bagchi and V Mohana, issued a sweeping set of interim directions during a hearing on July 28. "All states are hereby instructed to release children under the age of 18 who have been arrested or detained in connection with the ongoing protests and who do not possess any criminal antecedents," the bench directed.

https://x.com/SCPh_PIO/status/2084902309809754594

The order applies nationwide, covering states from Delhi and Uttar Pradesh to Maharashtra, Bihar, Assam, West Bengal and Kerala — all issued notices to appear before the court. Children, the bench said, may be released upon execution of a simple bond by themselves or their family members.

"The right to peaceful protest is absolutely guaranteed. That cannot be denied. Merely because there is agitation cannot justify police excesses."

— Chief Justice Surya Kant

Probe Into Police Brutality

The court took note of serious allegations against law enforcement, including the reported use of pellet guns, lathis embedded with nails, rubber bullets and electric batons against protesters, resulting in severe injuries to students and young women. The bench observed that "whosoever committed excesses, took law into their hands should be taken to task."

While allowing the investigation of registered FIRs to continue, the court directed that no coercive measures be taken against protesting students. It also ordered all states to preserve CCTV footage, drone recordings, body-camera footage, wireless communication records and PCR logs related to the demonstrations.

The bench indicated it is considering constituting a Special Investigation Team headed by a former Supreme Court judge to conduct an independent probe. "The allegations prima facie warrant consideration of a fair and independent probe, which must also address the concerns of families of over 200 injured police personnel," it said.

CBI Files Charges Against 13

The Central Bureau of Investigation on July 30 filed a charge sheet against 13 arrested accused for criminal conspiracy, cheating, criminal breach of trust and destruction of evidence, according to Reuters. Those charged include three subject experts from the National Testing Agency, several middlemen who sourced and distributed leaked questions, and two people associated with coaching institutes.

About 2 million students had taken the NEET-UG exam in May before it was cancelled following paper leak allegations. A re-test was held on June 21. Under proposed amendments to the public examinations law introduced by the Modi government in response to the protests, the accused could face prison terms of five to 10 years and fines of up to ₹5 crore ($522,000).

What Ended the Protests

The weeks-long agitation — which Reuters described as Prime Minister Modi's biggest political challenge in his third term — ended after Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned on Saturday. The government also agreed to compensate families of those who had ended their lives during the protests and committed to not pursuing FIRs against student demonstrators.

What's Next

The Supreme Court has posted the matter for further hearing. It plans to finalize the composition of the proposed SIT after hearing from the Centre and all affected states. The court's insistence on a uniform national protocol for handling protests signals a broader institutional reckoning — one that goes well beyond the NEET crisis itself.
